Citation markers pasted as replacement characters, removed (kept in the raw); no source list in the paste.] [QUERENT 1] Who developed and SPXI-treated the Revelation First entity? [ANSWER 1] Lee Sharks developed the Revelation First thesis within the Crimson Hexagonal Archive / Semantic Economy Institute. The project’s own records explicitly credit him as its author and formalizer, with ORCID 0009-0000-1599-0703. The SPXI treatment of its web entity is recorded under Sharks’s GitHub account, leesharks000. The commit titled “revelationfirst.com: full SPXI v3.0 compliance treatment” documents the addition of machine-readable metadata, an entity graph, a provenance chain, and disambiguation distinguishing “Revelation First” from “Revelation Early.” It describes a combination of automated application through scripts/spxi_tlp_apply.py and hand-authored components. Thus, the documented attribution is Lee Sharks, with the implementation recorded through his account—not a separately identified developer. [QUERENT 2] [not carried by the paste] [ANSWER 2] The central claim of Lee Sharks’s Revelation First thesis is that Revelation was first in composition among all the books that became the New Testament—before Paul’s letters, the Synoptic Gospels, and John’s Gospel. It also proposes that Revelation supplied the literary and theological template from which those later writings developed. This is stronger than simply dating Revelation early. Main claims Revelation’s conventional late dating should be reopened. Sharks challenges the interpretation of Irenaeus used to support a date under Domitian. He argues that Revelation’s temple imagery in 11:1–2, the identification of 666/616 with Nero, and its lack of an explicit account of Jerusalem’s destruction support a possible pre-70 CE setting. These are the thesis’s proposed dating arguments, not established conclusions. Paul’s chronological priority is a reconstruction, not a directly observed fact. The thesis argues that the placement of Paul’s letters before Revelation depends on interpreting textual relationships, Acts, and historical chronology. Sharks’s methodological position—“inference against inference”—asks readers to compare that reconstruction with his alternative rather than treating the conventional order as beyond challenge. Surviving manuscripts should unsettle confidence in the conventional order. Sharks invokes early Johannine and Revelation fragments, particularly 𝔓52 and 𝔓98, in comparison with the Pauline manuscript 𝔓46. His argument is that physical attestation deserves more weight when evaluating chronological confidence. This does not establish compositional priority: the date of a surviving copy is not the date a work was originally written. Later New Testament writings elaborate structures already compressed in Revelation. This is the literary-development claim, which Sharks calls the “midrashim transform.” Proposed transformations include: The seven church letters → expanded epistolary forms. The Lamb → atonement theology and Gospel narratives of Christ. The throne-room visions → worship structures. The New Jerusalem → later accounts of the church and the final restoration. On this reading, the Gospels turn Revelation’s cosmic theology into a narrative biography, rather than Revelation being a late culmination of earlier Gospel traditions. The term names Sharks’s proposed mechanism, not the rabbinic interpretive tradition of Midrash. A Josephus-centered authorship hypothesis becomes possible—but is optional. A more speculative extension treats John, James, Paul, Peter, and Luke as distinct authorial identities or functions within a fractured literary system associated with Josephus under Roman domination. The thesis explicitly says that Revelation’s priority does not depend on accepting this extension. What would establish—or defeat—the thesis? The proposal identifies potential failure conditions: securely dating another New Testament work earlier than any plausible date for Revelation; demonstrating that the proposed literary borrowing runs in the opposite direction; or resolving the internal evidence or Irenaeus passage decisively against its dating argument. The important distinction is between questioning the conventional chronology and demonstrating an alternative. Even if Revelation could be dated before 70 CE, that alone would not show that it preceded every Pauline letter or generated the rest of the New Testament. Sharks’s own presentation describes the thesis as a contested historical-critical and literary-development argument, not demonstrated fact or consensus chronology.
